A single Sole Source NYPD contract for 911 computer-aided dispatch, and one of the largest lines on the page. The class is right but the substitution question is mostly formal: mission-critical CAD has no credible open-source replacement, so the real levers are the sole-source renewal terms and vendor risk - Hexagon (which acquired Intergraph in 2010) spun the dispatch division out into Octave in 2026, so the counterparty and roadmap changed mid-term.

Held by DoITT and criminal justice agencies. NICE is the vendor name, not one product: the contracts buy its public-safety suite - NICE Inform for 911 logging and recording, NICE Investigate/Evidencentral for digital evidence. Kept as one family because the products share a vendor relationship and a function. No open-source substitute exists for evidentiary-grade 911 logging, so the working lever is the Sole Source and Amendment renewal terms.

Over 2 NYPD renewals for acoustic gunshot detection. This is a vendor-operated sensor network with monitoring and alerting delivered as a service - hosting in the 'someone else runs it' sense, with no public rate card. Commercial pricing is quoted per square mile of coverage, so the checkable figure is cost per covered area against other cities' published contracts. Same vendor as the $46.1M Casebuilder line: one relationship near $90M, kept as two families because they are genuinely different products.

On a single renewal held by the Office of Contract Services: Ivalua is the platform underneath PASSPort, the City's own procurement portal - including the contract records this analysis reads. Bespoke SaaS with no public rate card and switching costs near the maximum possible, so the benchmark lever is soft; what is checkable at renewal is scope, per-module pricing and the implementation-services share of the bill.

On one GSA contract at the Department of Social Services. A cited identity check found this is a managed contact-center service and systems-integration deal, not a proprietary product - the software underneath is NICE CXone, operated for the agency by C1 (formerly ConvergeOne). It stays in the hosting class because the purchase is 'someone else runs it', and contact-center-as-a-service is one of the rare bespoke categories with public benchmarks: usage-priced competitors publish rate cards, so cost per agent seat and per minute is a checkable figure.

Bought separately across many agencies - virtual apps and desktops, NetScaler load balancing and ShareFile, bought separately (8 of 11 via MWBE small purchase). The substitution question is real but partial: the catalogue maps remote access to Apache Guacamole at partial confidence, and nothing maps the NetScaler or virtualization estate. The nearer-term question is fragmentation - 8 agencies buying one vendor's portfolio on 11 separate contracts.

On one GSA contract at DoITT for citywide streetscape imagery. This buys data - periodic capture of street-level imagery and derived products - not software, so a substitute product is the wrong question. The content questions are the real ones: capture frequency against actual refresh need, overlap with imagery the City already commissions, and whether usage justifies citywide coverage.

The legacy CA Technologies portfolio - mainframe systems management, the CA-IDMS database, Erwin data modeling - bought through resellers since Broadcom acquired CA in 2018. Recorded purposes mix licenses with maintenance and support, and on a shrinking platform the two are inseparable: nobody adopts CA-IDMS today, they pay to keep it running. The lever is not a support tier or a substitute; it is the mainframe exit timeline - every renewal should carry a date question, not just a price one.

A single Department of Finance renewal for property tax administration. Specialized government software with a thin vendor market and no open-source equivalent - the catalogue has nothing in property assessment - so the substitution lever is formal only. The function view is where this spend should be read: property assessment shows 4 products across 4 agencies doing adjacent parts of the same tax job.

On one NYPD amendment for WebFOCUS business intelligence and reporting - a legacy BI platform at a single agency. Citywide, the BI and dashboards function already spans 6 products across 9 agencies, so the practical question is consolidation onto the City's mainstream BI stack rather than a like-for-like swap; open-source BI exists, but the migration cost is the accumulated report estate, not the license.

Bought separately across many agencies, mostly on GSA schedule - the strongest substitution case in the whole analysis: the catalogue maps ArcGIS Desktop and Pro to QGIS at strong confidence, with 69 government adopters. The split matters: ArcGIS Server maps only to GeoServer at partial, so desktop seats and server infrastructure are different migration projects with different risk. See the replacement candidates on this page.

Bought separately by NYPD, Emergency Management, Homeless Services, Social Services and others each subscribing separately to the same real-time event-alerting feed. This is a data service, not software: the product is the alerts. Two questions: whether each agency's subscription earns its keep (the classic content question), and why five agencies hold fifteen separate short-term contracts for one feed rather than a citywide agreement.

A single NYPD renewal with IDEMIA for automated fingerprint identification (AFIS) and biometric storage. No open-source substitute exists; the vendor market is a handful of global biometric firms, so the working lever is competitive re-procurement among them at renewal rather than substitution - and the data-portability terms that make re-procurement possible at all.

At Environmental Protection, Buildings and Correction - enterprise asset management (Infor EAM) plus Infor Public Sector ERP and permitting. One caution from the cited identity check: Infor sold the standalone EAM product line to Hexagon in 2021, so part of this family's product now belongs to a different vendor and renewal paperwork may not match the original nameplate. The facilities and maintenance function shows 4 products across 6 agencies - a crowded field.

Via Carahsoft for legal matter management. A cited identity check found LegalStratus is a Salesforce-based application acquired by Litify in 2021 - the license rides the Salesforce platform, so the dependency to price is two vendors deep. Legal case management citywide spans 11 products across 7 agencies; that fragmentation, not substitution, is the actionable finding.

Commissary ordering for the Department of Correction. ⚠ MIND WHO PAYS: commissary systems in correctional settings are commonly funded from incarcerated people's purchases and commissary revenue rather than from tax levy, and the vendor's revenue can be tied to transaction volume. The Homeless Management Information System and data warehouse for DSS/DHS. The realistic move is new work in R/Python while the existing estate is retired, and the fragmentation across agencies is itself worth consolidating first.

Assigned-counsel case tracking and voucher payment for the Office of Criminal Justice, supporting the 18-B panel of court-appointed defence attorneys. A bespoke government workflow - case assignment plus attorney payment - with no comparable product to substitute; the question is whether the system's cost is proportionate to the panel it administers, and whether voucher processing could ride existing City payment infrastructure.

Workers' compensation case management. ⚠ Read together with ClaimsVISION, which does the same job for the same kind of claim: two workers' compensation systems is a consolidation question, and the per-product view cannot ask it. Computer-assisted mass appraisal for the Department of Finance. ⚠ Read together with the Tyler Technologies Property Tax System, also at Finance: assessment and tax administration are adjacent halves of one function bought from two vendors. The property-assessment field has no open-source entrant in the catalogue, so the useful question is the boundary between the two systems and what each is authoritative for.

Behavioural health data and resource management for DOHMH. A hosted registry/directory of behavioural health providers and resources. ⚠ The comparison worth making is internal: the City runs several service-directory and referral systems, and a resource directory is among the most duplicated kinds of system in government. Ask what distinguishes this one before renewing it.

Child-welfare data reporting and monitoring for ACS. Reporting and analytics delivered as a hosted service over data ACS already holds - which is the question: this is dashboards over the City's own child-welfare records, and the City has its own BI capability (the function view shows several BI platforms already licensed). Ask what the vendor adds beyond the reporting layer.

Secondhand and pawnshop transaction records for NYPD investigations. ⚠ This is access to a vendor-operated NATIONAL DATABASE, not software the City could run: the value is other jurisdictions' data, which is precisely why substitution is impossible and why the price is not benchmarkable against a rate card. The lever is usage - how many investigations actually query it - which this data cannot show.

Emergency mass notification and critical-event management. ⚠ Read together with AlertMedia, already curated, which does the same job: two mass-notification platforms is exactly the duplication the cross-agency function view exists to surface. Notification is priced per contact or per message and several vendors publish tiers, so it is genuinely benchmarkable - and the open-source commons has nothing here, which the page records as a gap.

Facilities, space and maintenance management bought separately by several agencies. ⚠ Its largest contracts run through resellers and integrators rather than the vendor, so the vendor table understates the relationship. A computerised maintenance management system has no credible open-source substitute at this scale; the fragmentation across agencies is the nearer question, and it sits in the same facilities function as MRI Software and AssetWorks.

Electronic patient care reporting for FDNY emergency medical services. Prehospital ePCR is a regulated clinical record feeding state EMS reporting, so substitution is constrained by certification rather than by capability. The question is integration - whether the record flows into the receiving hospital and the state registry without re-entry - not price.

Electronic signature and contract lifecycle management, bought separately by many agencies. ⚠ THIS IS THE CLEAREST CONSOLIDATION CANDIDATE IN THIS PASS: one commodity capability, many agencies, many separate contracts, and e-signature is priced per envelope or per seat with published tiers - so both a citywide agreement and a price benchmark are available. The open-source commons has credible e-signature options, making this one of the few rows where substitution is a real question rather than a formality.

Historical and current property mapping data. This is archival CONTENT - digitised fire-insurance atlases and property records - so the substitution question is about the source. ⚠ Much of the underlying historical material is public-domain and some is already digitised by libraries and the City's own records agency; the question is whether the City is paying for access to material it holds elsewhere.

Workers' compensation claims management, recorded as maintenance and support rather than new licence. ⚠ Read together with Conduent StrataWare, which does the same job: before asking about the support tier, ask why two systems administer the same class of claim. Support on a system the City may be consolidating away from is the weakest kind of renewal.

Construction program and project management for capital work. ⚠ Read together with ProContrl and the other construction-management systems in the capital program: capital project controls are bought repeatedly across the agencies that build things. Hosted project controls are priced per project or per user with published tiers, so the price is checkable; the scope overlap across agencies is the larger question.

Network security and firewall support across several agencies. Firewall support is a legitimate purchase - the question is tier and appliance count, not substitution, since the hardware is already in place. ⚠ Network security is the most fragmented function on the whole page (the function view shows dozens of distinct products across most agencies), so this row is worth reading as one line in that picture rather than on its own.

Laboratory information management for clinical and public-health labs. ⚠ Read together with LabVantage LIMS, also a LIMS and also in the City's laboratories: two laboratory information systems is a consolidation question, though the answer may legitimately be no - forensic and public-health labs carry different accreditation regimes. Open-source LIMS exist but rarely carry the required accreditation, so substitution is constrained by certification.

Payment processing. ⚠ THE LEVER HERE IS A RATE, NOT A LICENCE: payment processing is priced as a percentage of transaction value plus a per-transaction fee, all of it publicly published, so this is among the most precisely benchmarkable lines in the inventory - and at City transaction volumes a fraction of a percent is real money. Ask what rate the City is paying against published interchange-plus pricing, and how it compares to the City's other payment channels.

Application performance monitoring. ⚠ Read together with the other monitoring platforms already licensed - SolarWinds, Splunk and several infrastructure monitors appear separately in the function view - because observability is a function the City buys repeatedly. Priced per host or per monitored unit with published tiers, so it is benchmarkable, and credible open-source observability stacks exist.

Laboratory information management for forensic biology at the Chief Medical Examiner. Forensic LIMS carries chain-of-custody and accreditation requirements that general laboratory software does not, so substitution is genuinely constrained here - more so than for STARLIMS. Read the two together as one laboratory-systems question, while respecting that a forensic lab may legitimately need its own.

Document and enterprise content management, bought separately by several agencies under many product spellings (Documentum, Liquid Office and others merged here). ⚠ The merge is the point: this reads as one vendor relationship spread across agencies and product lines, and content management is a function with credible open-source options in the catalogue. Ask whether the City needs several ECM platforms - this family, Alfresco and Accellion all appear separately - before asking about any one of them.

Housing asset management. ⚠ Read alongside Archibus and AssetWorks: three families in this pass manage property, facilities or assets, in different agencies, with overlapping capability. Specialised housing-management software has no open-source substitute, so the useful question is the boundary between these systems rather than replacing any of them.

column5: Log management and security monitoring, bought by several agencies - every one through the MWBE small-purchase route and through a different reseller, so it reads as several small buys of one platform rather than a citywide agreement. ⚠ THE LEVER IS THE PRICING MODEL, not the licence: Splunk is licensed by data volume ingested per day (with a newer compute-based model alongside it), so cost tracks how much log data is pointed at it - which means routing noisy sources elsewhere reduces the bill without losing capability. Ask what is being ingested before asking what it costs. ⚠ Its catalogue match is Grafana at `partial`, which understates the field: Grafana is visualisation, while the credible open-source comparators for this job are the OpenSearch/Elasticsearch stack (catalogued separately here) and Wazuh for the security-monitoring half. The classifier rated its own contracts inconsistently - low on three, medium on three - so the page shows a distribution rather than a verdict.

Secure file transfer and sharing for the Law Department, DoITT and ACS, bought through three resellers on two routes. ⚠ WHAT A RENEWAL SHOULD CHECK HERE IS ASSURANCE, NOT PRICE. The vendor's LEGACY product, Accellion FTA, was breached in late 2020 and early 2021 by groups linked to CLOP, exposing client data and settling for $8.1M; the vendor states Kiteworks - the product the City buys - is a separate codebase and was not affected, and Mandiant's report on the FTA attack is published. ⚠ That history is context, not an allegation about this product: state it as the reason to ask for current assurance evidence (authorisation status, penetration-test cadence) at renewal, which matters more than the unit price for a tool whose whole purpose is moving sensitive material safely. Read alongside Box and the other file-sharing lines: the City licenses several ways to move files, and secure transfer has credible open-source options.

Document processing recorded as Optical Character Recognition for the Department of Finance, bought Sole Source from Tyler Technologies. ⚠ SAME VENDOR AS THE TYLER PROPERTY TAX SYSTEM, also at Finance and also effectively sole-sourced - so one vendor holds two of Finance's systems, which is a relationship worth seeing whole rather than as two rows. ⚠ AND THE RECORDED PURPOSE MAY UNDERSTATE THE PRODUCT: plain OCR is among the most commoditised capabilities in software, with mature open-source engines and cloud APIs priced per page, so if this really is OCR the price deserves hard questions. Tyler's Intellidact is in practice a records-processing workflow - classification, redaction and indexing of recorded documents - which is a different and more defensible purchase. Establishing which of the two the City is actually buying is the first question, and it is not answerable from this data.
